subtopic: NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF CULTURAL EDUCATION CENTRES
NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF CULTURAL EDUCATION CENTRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recent federal government cuts in spending are threatening the very existence of important First Nations programs like those that deal with culture.
May 4, 1993

Cuts to the National Association of Cultural Education Centres will affect the operations of the national organization and its 72 centres across Canada. One of the centres hardest hit is the one in Saskatchewan which serves all First Nations people in my province from its office in Saskatoon.
The First Nations cultural program has been serving aboriginal people since 1972. It began because of the recognition that culture is an integral part of learning. This is so important that the national association is promoting legislation that would protect and safeguard the cultural interests of First Nations people.
I support this important and decentralized initiative which delivers programs dealing with culture, language, history and heritage to people at the local level. I condemn the federal government for cutting the funding which makes this possible.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Association of Elizabeth Fry Societies is a federation of 21 community based groups dedicated to the provision of programs and services to women in the criminal justice system.
At the national level the society works toward longterm law reform and social change. It is also committed to providing increased opportunities for federally sentenced women to speak so that their voices are not silenced.
The majority of women in conflict with the law has experienced various forms of violence: physical, psychological and/or sexual. Many have experienced racism and poverty. This violence is peqretuated by a system which all too often works against the needs of women. The separation from family and inadequate legal representation are but two examples. The result is further disem-powerment of women and lack of healing.
The aim of Elizabeth Fry Week is to raise public awareness of the situation of women in the criminal justice system. Greater awareness will in turn encourage greater exploration of alternative ideas to end the cycles of violence which further victimize women involved in the criminal justice system.
We salute Elizabeth Fry Week.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to pay tribute to a distinguished Canadian who passed away late last week. The Hon. Colin Bennett made an outstanding contribution to Canada as a parliamentarian, as a judge and as a respected business leader.
Colin Bennett was born in 1908 in the town of Meaford, Ontario where he attended public school before graduating with a degree in political economy trom Victoria College at the University of Toronto in 1931. After attending Osgoode Hall Law School he was called to the bar in 1936 and he returned to Meaford to practise with the law firm of Albery and Bennett.
A veteran of the Second World War, he served in the Royal Canadian Air Force from 1941 to 1945 and retired with the rank of group captain.
Colin Bennett was first elected to this House as the Liberal member of Parliament for Grey North in 1949.
He sought election after many years of public service including the time that he spent as town clerk and solicitor, as chairman of the board of stewards of Meaford United Church, as manager of the Meaford Intermediate Baseball Team, as president of the Meaford Curling Club, as a master in the Masonic Lodge, as secretary of the Meaford Chamber of Commerce and as a member of the board of Meaford Hospital.
My colleague for Bruce-Grey and I are very privileged to follow such an outstanding individual as representatives in this House for Grey County. During his time in this House he was Canada's representative on the Legal Committee and alternate delegate to the General Assembly at the United Nations in Paris in 1951. He served as Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs in 1953 and was appointed as a Queen's Counsel in 1956.
After serving eight years in the House of Commons, Mr. Bennett left Parliament before the 1957 election when he was appointed to the bench at the County Court of Grey County. He went on to become Chief Judge of the County and District Courts of Ontario and was the first chairman of the Criminal Injuries Compensation Board where he was active as an arbiter and conciliator in labour disputes.
He also was a leading member of the business community when, after resigning from the bench in 1974, he served as president and later as honorary chairman of the Victoria and Grey Trust Company, now known as National Trust.
I am hard pressed to think of anyone who gave so tirelessly to his community and to his country as did Colin Bennett. He represents everything that is good about this country and set a very high standard for those of us who followed him in this House.
His accomplishments in public life, while extraordinary, were not his greatest achievement. His role as a husband, father and grandfather is what gave him the most pride and satisfaction. He is survived by his wife, Fern, and the three children, Cynthia, Laurence and Mary Ellen.
It is to them that I would like to not only pass on the sincere condolences of this House and of the people of Grey County, but rather I would like to thank them for giving him the personal and family support that allowed him to make such an extraordinary contribution to this community and to Canada.
Colin Bennett will be greatly missed.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pay tribute from this side of the House to a former member of this House, Colin Emerson Bennett.
He was born in Grey County, Meaford, Ontario, attended the public and high schools there, the University of Toronto and Osgoode Hall. He was called to the bar in 1936 and practised law in Meaford on his graduation. He served this country with the Royal Canadian Air Force from 1941 to 1945 and attained the rank of group captain. In 1949 he was elected to this House for Grey North and he was re-elected in 1953. From 1953 to 1957 he served as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. On April 15, 1957 he was appointed judge in the County Court of the County of Grey in the province of Ontario.
Mr. Bennett was popular as a politician and a judge. As a judge he was witty but meticulously fair. In the early 1960s he was promoted to chief judge for Ontario. In the early 1970s upon leaving the bench he was made chief executive officer for Victoria and Grey Trust. In 1982 he was made honorary chairman of the board.
Colin Bennett will be missed by his family including his grandchildren. I extend to them our condolences from this side of the House. Colin Bennett spent a lifetime serving his community, amateur sports, his county and his country. His contribution has made Canada a better place for all of us.

Mr. Speaker, budgets provide an opportunity for government to account to the country on the spending, the anticipated spending and the programs for the upcoming year.
This particular budget was really an annual accounting because the bulk of the changes made that would have normally been made in this budget were made earlier, indeed last year in the financial statement of December. This budget has to be read with the December financial statement to indicate the totality of the government's attack on a very serious problem: the effect of a recession and a very serious restructuring. It is not easy to deal with problems. Our debts have been growing exponentially, but this budget keeps us on track and still forecasts the deficit at $32.6 billion for the current year.
There have been all sorts of suggestions, and indeed I have made them myself, that we should have had a budget with a whole host of methods by which we could more seriously attack the public debt.
I might point out this budget in its forecasts estimates that we will not have to borrow fresh money from the marketplace after 1997-98.
Be that as it may, I believe it will probably be necessary for the new government under a new Prime Minister,

The people of this country are not going to vote for a political party that at the same time as our debt is being attacked and our financial figures are being attacked votes to spend $20 billion a year more on a national child care program, $15 billion on a further infrastructure program and more on a national jobs plan. This budget could have done a number of things but all of those things would have required extensive legislative change. For example, we could start priorizing some of our expenditures. We would have to have a real priorizing effort. We could have a conference. We could have a finance committee meeting. We could have a session in this House about priorizing expenditures. The fact of the matter is that we cannot afford all the government we presently have. The country does not have the sufficient ability to raise revenue, to pay taxes, to pay for all of the government we presently enjoy and pay the debt.
We will have to priorize our expenditures. That priori-zation will take legislation. It will take the elimination of programs, the rejigging and re-tailoring of programs, and the restructuring of our whole economic system from the federal point of view.
We could attack transfers to the provinces. The Prime Minister earlier today said there was something like $43 billion transferred to the provinces for medicare, postsecondary education, Canada Assistance Plan and equalization. He will probably remember when the present government was put into office in 1984 the question was whether it was going to cut expenditures. The promise in that election was that a new Conservative government under the Prime Minister would cut expenditures and balance the budget.

It will lay the foundation for the next budget and the next government. It had nine years to balance the budget. The government has not done it and the Liberals have not done it in the past. Why should people in Canada now believe that any of the parties are able or willing to cut expenditures and not just say they cannot because of transfer payments and this and that.
The hon. member knows very well that if there is a will it can be done. Naturally I believe if he had been Minister of Finance instead of the present Minister of Finance he would have done it but he is not and I do not think he will be.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member and I know each other fairly well and I always enjoy his comments.
I want to say that this is not an easy matter. The government has tried for a long period of time to grow out of the deficit by curtailing expenditures bit by bit and it has done that. It has curtailed an enormous number of expenditures but the things the Government of Canada does today are infinitely smaller than the number of things it attempted to do when it took office.
Unfortunately the debt compounds and it is in a situation where compounding debt requires action much more serious than it has had before. Part of the problem of course is the fact that there is a serious recession. Consequently income is way off. Tax revenues, as the hon. member will know, are off at least $10 billion from what was forecasted for this year. That $10 billion makes
May 4, 1993

an enormous difference in the debt position of the country.
Incomes for individuals are off. People are not earning and that means they are not spending and paying goods and services tax for example. The problem is that payments are being made to support a social net structure to keep people going at the same as there is a great reduction in income.
I do not think it is going to get that much easier. We are going to have to do some really hard thinking to break the cycle of debt.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to designate tomorrow as an allotted day.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in this debate today. Perhaps I should just remind members and those who may be paying attention via the television about the motion that we are debating today. It is an opposition day motion and it says:
Thai this House is of the opinion that the Budget is, as put by the
Chief Government Whip, "a disgrace".
I think it is a good thing that such a motion was found to be in order because it permits us to debate the budget and also to call attention to the fact that there seems to be a division of opinion on the other side as to the merit of the budget which just goes to show that these things happen. It just goes to show that there is a variety of opinion in all caucuses on a great many things.
I think it is interesting that the government Whip said this but I do not want to dwell too much on that. I think what happened with this budget is that we basically had a budget so that the government could not be accused of not having a budget. That was basically the only purpose that the budget served. Had it not brought in a budget because it did not want to saddle a new Prime Minister and a new leader of the Conservative Party with a real budget, it would have been open to criticism for leaving the country budgetless. It brought in something and called it a budget. By doing so it deflected any criticism that might have originated in that vein.
I do not think that they have been able to avoid legitimate criticism because in spite of the fact that it was
Supply
not much of a budget there were measures in there that are nonetheless objectionable. There were other things that could have been in there and we objected to their absence.
I will start with some of the things that we find objectionable. It is something that I have spoken on in this House many times. It has to do with the continuing attack by this government on VIA Rail, which is the passenger rail service in this country. I believe the budget said that there would be a $50 million cutback and then a $100 million cutback per year thereafter.
What does this tell everybody who lives outside the Montreal-Windsor corridor? It tells them basically that passenger rail service anywhere outside that corridor, where there is a slim chance of making a profit, is expendable. It says that the rest of the country does not really count and that commitments made by this government-as a government and when the Conservatives were in opposition-over the years to the maintenance of a passenger rail service in this country have proven to be rather empty.
It is not as if this is the first thing it has ever done. I am sure we will recall the great evil that was done to VIA Rail in the announcements made in the fall of 1989 that took effect on January 15, 1990. I would remind the House that despite promises to the contrary and implications to the contrary that many people who lost service at that time, thanks to those cuts, still have not had their needs met.
I am thinking particularly of people in my riding who for many years were able to access their summer cottages by rail and are no longer able to do that in the way that they used to. We are now entering into the fourth or fifth summer and some of those people still cannot access their cottages because the promises that were made by various ministers of transport to enable, facilitate and to fund alternate modes of travel such as roads have still not come to pass.
I am not in favour of these alternate modes except in the absence of a return to the rail service. I would prefer that we saw the wisdom, not of constantly paring back passenger rail service, but of finding ways to use the train more and not less.

May 4, 1993
Supply
I say this not because I happen to represent an area which is identified with rail service and has a rail shop in it but because environmental reasons show this as the way to go.
It is a form of perverted bookkeeping to say that we are saving money over here by cutting back on VIA Rail and at the same time opening up areas through the eventual building of roads that were to this point not opened up in that way. This will put more people on the Trans-Canada Highway between Winnipeg and the Mi-naki road, increase traffic, increase hydrocarbon emissions and cause all those things that are harmful in the name of saving dollars in one set of books.
What we do not do and what budgets seem incapable of doing, at least to this point, is to keep that big set of books. We are not doing what might be called metabookkeeping. We need to do that if we are going to take into account both the effect of budget measures on the environment and the effect of budget measures on social reality and the social costs that come with particular government measures.
I talked a bit about what is in the budget and concentrated mostly on the VIA Rail end of it. I would also like to talk about what was not in the budget. This budget, like every other Tory budget before it, was very heavily laden with the rhetoric of deficit reduction.
One of the things that we have pressed, and I have particularly pressed the government on as the NDP tax critic is to say if it is serious about reducing the deficit and it wants to demonstrate that seriousness and have credibility with ordinary Canadians when it comes to deficit reduction, then it has to show that it is prepared to ask something of not so ordinary Canadians-the rich in this country and the corporate elite-particular sacrifices in order to reduce the deficit.
When it has done that and it is still able to show that it has a deficit problem then it will have what I consider as the moral high ground. It will be able to say: "We have done that and we still have a problem".
That is not what this government has done. It has not demanded those sacrifices from the people who have a great deal to sacrifice and a great deal to give to the common treasury.
There are a number of examples. Not too long ago we went through a debate in this House that was eventually brought to an end by closure with respect to the way in which private family trusts were having their capital gains tax exemption extended beyond the 21 years that was given to them in 1972 by the Liberals.
There was an opportunity for the government to show that it is not just ordinary Canadians that have to pay up in order to reduce the deficit but people who have the good fortune to have these private family trusts. In some cases they have tens of millions of dollars in these family trusts but were they asked to make a contribution in this way? No, they were not.
Other tax loopholes have been identified over the last several years many of which I raised in this House with the Minister of Finance before the budget for instance.
I mentioned the business and entertainment tax deduction. I realize that this is a controversial suggestion. Many people in the restaurant business think that this would be harmful to them but I would say that it probably depends on which part of the country one comes from and maybe even which part of the city one comes from. I am sure that most of the restaurants in my riding do not depend on business men being able to deduct the cost of their lunch from their taxes. They depend on the business of ordinary folk coming in and using their restaurant because it is a good restaurant, because they like to eat out or whatever the case may be. I thought that the government might have looked at that. I understand that it is being looked at south of the border.
So often in this House we hear that we cannot do things because they are not doing it in the United States and therefore we would be uncompetitive. Competitive so often seems to mean a sort of uncritical imitation. Nevertheless this is changing in the United States. I thought I heard from the Minister of Finance at one point when I raised this that maybe he was looking at this. I was genuinely disappointed when the budget came down that he had not at least tried to reduce it. Maybe he felt that he could not eliminate it, but it could have been reduced to 80 per cent or 50 per cent.
May 4. 1993

This has been done away with in other countries and all the restaurants have not boarded up their windows and gone out of business. There was $1 billion. One might ask what is $1 billion when it comes to the kind of deficits we are talking about. It all adds up. It not only adds up but it gives credibility to the government when it is asking sacrifices of other people. Certainly $1 billion more than covers the money that the government is going to extract by cutting back on VIA Rail, the CBC and other institutions that have helped define Canada over the years. I think Canadians value these things a whole lot more than they value the opportunity of the business community to deduct their lunches or their season tickets at the Forum or the Skydome or whatever the case may be on their income tax returns. There was a choice that could have been made but was not made.
Tax loopholes were identified by the Auditor General in his most recent report. There is the way in which Canada is being used really by companies that borrow here and deduct the interest on the loan. They invest in some other country that is probably a low wage country, which is a tax haven in itself. They make a profit but do not pay any taxes because of this tax haven. They transfer the profits back here in the form of dividends and do not pay any taxes on that because of the dividend tax credit. There are all kinds of ways that people have of literally ripping off the Canadian public but in a very legal way.
The government could have moved to do something about that but it did not.
All of this says to me, as it says to so many other Canadians, that maybe the government is not serious about the debt and the deficit. Maybe, as we have always suspected on this side of the House, for every ounce of genuine concern about the debt or the deficit there is another ounce or two of political duplicity involved. It could be using the deficit to cover what is basically an ideological agenda and to do certain things that it would like to do anyway for a priori philosophical reasons that it does because of necessity and because it has no choice.
I think there are choices. I think that even when we do face genuine problems with deficits and debts there are still choices to be made. It is not just a question of necessity. It is also a question of, when one does arrive at
Supply
a situation where one has to address debt and deficit problems, how to do it and not just do something that one might otherwise want to do and justifying it by citing the debt or the deficit.
Where does the deficit come from? I think there is overwhelming evidence that much of this deficit is self-inflicted by the government. In particular I am thinking of the matter of interest rates and the way in which the government increased its own deficit by having the interest rate policy that it had for years. This goes back before even this particular government. I will get to this later if I have the time. In particular, to the extent that we owed the debt to ourselves, that was the extent to which our own interest rate policy was self-inflicting and compounding a debt on the country.
Not so long ago a Statistics Canada study showed that up to 50 per cent of the debt was attributable to that kind of expense. Another 44 per cent was attributable to revenue forgone in the form of the tax loopholes I have just spoken about. It is not just the ones I have spoken about but many others, most of which were created by Liberal governments in the seventies. Six per cent of the deficit was created by social spending.
Why is it that social spending is always being made the scapegoat? I go back to my earlier point that it is an ideological agenda. It may be that once we have the problem we cannot go back and change the interest rate policy. We cannot go back and recover all the money we have lost through revenue forgone thanks to tax loopholes, although we can close those loopholes and begin to collect the money now.
It may be that a government in a tight spot has to look at all kinds of spending, including certain forms of social spending, but it should not do it in the context of having blamed these programs in the first place.
Yet that is what has happened because it suits the philosophical frame of mind of so many people on the other side of the House who never liked these programs to be begin with. This is why they do not have any credibility when they attack them and when they cut back on them. Nobody really believes they actually regard this as a painful exercise.

I do not see any pain in their faces. All I see is joy. It is concealed sometimes, barely concealed, straining not to smile while they are announcing what they are doing to family allowances, to VIA Rail, to some Crown corporation, or to some other element of the Canadian fabric which a majority of Canadians accept but which Conservatives have always regarded as part of the problem with Canada. They are trying to get rid of all those so-called problems that have distinguished us from our neighbour to the south and make us more like the America that so many on the other side, particularly the Prime Minister, wished they were citizens of and have acted like they were citizens of ever since he became Prime Minister.
What about free trade? Is it just a coincidence that Ontario in particular but Canada in general has had all these economic problems in the-last two or three years or that the manufacturing sector has been gutted? It is not just the recession. It is a fundamental restructuring of the North American economy thanks to the free trade agreement. To the extent we even talk about the recession, we are using language which conceals rather than reveals what is really going on.
I am not going to talk about the recession any more. I am going to talk about the free trade agreement. Often on the other side we hear that the recession is not just in Canada but is global. Yes, the recession is global because not just this government but the United States, the British, the European and many other governments have been following the same kind of neo-conservative policies throughout the 1980s. If we have a global recession it is no wonder. It is due to the adoption of policies not just by this government but by governments almost worldwide, even by governments that do not want to adopt the policies but have them forced on them by the IMF, the World Bank or others that demand their particular view of life and its implementation be the condition of credit or any consideration by these international financial institutions.
I see you signalling, Mr Speaker. I assume that has something to do with my time expiring. I will try to wrap up, I have so much more to say. The fact is that I was hoping to get into the whole question of debt and deficit a little more thoroughly than I have had the opportunity to do.
One of the things people are coming to realize is that part of the problem with the deficit is the whole question of foreign borrowing. I was reading an article this weekend by Professor Rueben Bellan of the University of Winnipeg. He has always been a critic of those who have been in his view overly concerned about the deficit. He wrote a book about full employment and how employment rather than the deficit is the real problem. Even he, if I read him correctly, seems to be concerned about the question of foreign borrowing. His argument in the past has been that we owe this deficit to ourselves and therefore it is not as great a concern as some people have made it out to be.
I wonder if I might have the indulgence of the House to continue my argument for a few more minutes. Could you seek unanimous consent of the House, Mr. Speaker, just for a few more minutes?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent to give more time to the member?
Agreed.

I will not abuse the goodwill of the House. I was talking about the fact that Professor Reuben Bellan of Winnipeg sees a problem with the whole question of foreign borrowing. That is a distinction we did not make in the past because we owed so much of the money to ourselves and people like Professor Bellan used to argue that this was not a problem. That is the view we have traditionally taken in this corner of the House.
There are many ways in which foreign borrowing becomes a problem. Professor Bellan would argue that it makes us uncompetitive. Others have argued that it means in the final analysis, if the debt load to foreign borrowers is significant enough and gets out of hand, we are not governing and they are governing.
That is a fair point and I accept that point, given what I would regard as the sinful nature of international finance. This has become a fact for so many Third World countries, many of which have tried to operate outside the demands of those institutions and have failed, there is a point at which governments may want to make choices before choices are made for them. I would like to see the debt dealt with so we can do something about the environment, so we can have discretionary money to
May 4, 1993

clean up the planet. We will never clean up the planet if we do not have any disposable income to do it with.
There are some very pressing reasons why we need to get control of this situation and have money to spend but not on consumer items. We need to be talking about how we might use this so-called deficit crisis, because I still think that elements of it are exaggerated, to talk about a new global frugality, about the fact that we cannot live like we live now and not just fiscally. The whole world could not live like we live now because if the whole world lived like we live the planet would collapse next week.
We have to come to terms with things, not in terms of the deficit but in terms of our whole way of life and in terms of the whole image we have of the good life. That will be much more difficult than tackling any fiscal deficit that happens from year to year. If we could somehow mix those two tasks, if we could integrate those two tasks, and I am thinking on my feet now, we could be on the right road. Certainly that is what I will be giving my musings over to in the next little while.

Mr. Speaker, it is with interest that I listened to the distinguished member for Winnipeg Transcona. He touched some very important points. Maybe the last one was the most important, that is Canada's foreign debt. As we look at the statistics, probably in 1980 it was over $100 billion. Now it is about $300 billion that we owe foreigners, different countries. As the member said so well, once we lose control of our debt it goes into foreign hands and we lose control of the country.
If we do not address this problem, I do not think we will ever come out of the recession and we will never have control in Canada of our economic and social policies. They are going to be dictated by the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and others.
How can we come out of this situation? I think the first thing is to have a fiscally responsible government and policies. To do that I think we will, as some have said, have to tax those who can afford taxation. One of those is certainly big corporations that have not been paying adequate taxes in the past.
Supply
As well, we have to look at the situation globally and say: "Are we efficient as a country?" The member has touched on the question of VIA Rail and transportation.
I would like to ask him a question on that point because we have reduced our railway system. We have cut it off.
Most of our heavy traffic by rail goes through the United States. Naturally our railways are losing money. We are losing jobs and at the same time we have increased traffic on our highways. I do not think this is the way to go because we have a very cold climate and it is not an efficient mode of transportation.
Could the member elaborate on the question of the International Monetary Fund and as well on transportation?

Mr. Speaker, I would love to elaborate on the international financial institutions.
There is an interesting irony here. Basically what I was saying is that at some point debt becomes a sovereignty issue. People who are totally in hock to somebody else have no sovereignty, personally speaking. Countries that are totally in hock to someone else do not have any sovereignty.
The irony here is that you can either deal with your deficit in order to be independent of the international financial institutions or you can deal with your deficit because the international financial institutions have told you to deal with it.
It is two different spirits. If you are dealing with your deficit because the IMF, the World Bank or some New York bond rating institution or whatever have said you should behave in a certain way, then you are not increasing your sovereignty.
In a way you are doing what somebody else is telling you to do. I think that is what is wrong with the way the government has approached it. It has no commitment to economic sovereignty. It thinks that notions like economic sovereignty are either ideologically anathema or outdated.
Passe.

Passe. That is why they are able to enter into these free trade agreements. They want to see the most fundamental decisions about the economy made not by government but by the private sector and by the multinational corporate elite.

May 4, 1993
Supply
The difference between me and the government, if I was in charge of trying to eliminate the deficit, would be that we would be trying to eliminate the deficit so that the government that we were in charge of would have the money to act in a sovereign way and to re-establish some community input, control and values to our economic life.
People on the other side here want to get rid of the deficit not to do that. They want to do it for the same reason that they are willing to sign free trade agreements and talk uncritically about globalization and whatever. They think the people who run these international financial institutions are the people who you listen to. They think they are the people with real authority.
I say their authority is coercive and unacceptable. The reason I would like us to deal with the deficit is so that we never have to pay any attention to their particular view of the world ever again.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly enjoyed listening to the remarks of my colleague.
In the past few days we have been dealing with the budget that was introduced by this government. Whenever the opposition has criticized the fact that it does very little in reality of reducing the amount of debt and the debt burden, the government comes back and makes the claim that all the recommendations and efforts it has done in the past to reduce the deficit have all been voted against by this party. I would like to turn that around.
I know my colleague is a revenue critic and he has over the past numbers of years made recommendations and suggestions both in terms of expenditures like the helicopter program as well as on the revenue side in terms of tax changes. The changes that he has recommended would also have reduced the deficit.
My question to the hon. member is this: Is it fair to say that all the suggestions we have made that would reduce the deficit have been voted against and turned down by this government?

It is fair to say that every single suggestion that I have ever made to the Minister of Finance has not
been taken seriously. We will constantly hear: "Do you have an alternative, do you have an alternative?". We have suggested alternatives. Not only have they not been implemented but they have many times not even been dealt with substantively when they are raised on the floor of the House. That is the worst part.
The government is entitled to its view. It is entitled to its argument of why a particular tax loophole was better to have than to not have. But it is not even willing to engage most of the time in that kind of a debate, with the odd exception. I would say that sometimes the Minister of Finance has been willing to engage in that kind of debate-sometimes-depending on what I was raising.
Whenever I raised questions that really went to the heart of the matter, and that is the way in which the system is so stacked in favour of the really wealthy in this country, I would always get a non-answer. It was as if I had come too close; that there are certain things we are willing to talk about in this country and then there are other things where it is just as though you had never said them. I found that when I talked about the trusts. I found that when I have talked about a few other things.
Those trusts are sacred.

Some things are sacred in this country. You almost feel as if you have breached some kind of taboo, that there are some things you just should not talk about. When you do talk about them, it is like you had brought up the subject of sex in some kind of Victorian home, like you never said anything about it at all, that the word was never uttered, and life will carry on.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Calgary's debate on Friday I used some strong language to describe the apparent inconsistency between the fiscal and economic policies of two of my opponents for the leadership and what had emerged in the April 26 budget.
I termed that inconsistency "a disgrace". That is stronger language than I normally use, gentleman and consensus-builder that I am. Well, now, full of mischief and devoid of creativity, the hon. member for Willowdale has sought to fill the Liberal policy vacuum with a vacuous motion of his own.
May 4, 1993

I think it would be appropriate to set the record straight on what precisely was said in Calgary that has triggered this mischievous motion. I quote from the Calgary Herald of last Saturday:
Jim Edwards, the government Whip and MP for Edmonton Southwest, did his best to cement his standing as Alberta's local Tory hero by slamming Charest and Campbell for not insisting the federal budget take a tougher line on current government spending. The budget which included a forecast deficit of $35.5 billion and put aside all serious spending cuts until after the next election, is a good beginning but it does not go nearly far enough, said Edwards. "What I want to know is where were these two ministers when Maz drew up this budget" said Edwards, terming their conduct a disgrace.
The motion which we have before us today is framed, to put it gently, in inexactitude. I think it would be appropriate to stake out what is my position on the budget of April 26 since that is the subject of our debate today.
I quote from a statement I released the evening of the budget, April 26.
My first reaction to the budget speech of 1he hon. Don Mazankowski is one of support and co-operation. I am pleased at the tone and direction of the budget, the emphasis on expenditure cuts, deficit reduction and the renunciation of tax increases as an option to deal with Canada's fiscal issues.
While the measures are a move in the right direction, this budget does not go far enough. Our annual budget deficit is too high, our deficit to GNP ratio remains too high, our mounting debt level is too high. I remain convinced that real economic recovery, real job creation through the small business sector and rising income and standard of living for Canadians can only occur as our debt burden is lifted. I believe that greater fiscal prudence and action are required.
What must be done, what can be done? We must implement real fundamental restructuring based mainly on expenditure cuts to a minimum of $10 billion. Allow me to outline a basic plan for Canada.

First, a 10 per cent cut in salary for the Prime Minister, as a symbolic gesture; second, consolidation of departments and ministries of state to not more than 20; an immediate, in-depth review of Canada's defence policy, including a review of all public procurement options; an immediate freeze on Canada's financial support for the European Bank for Reconstruction and development; accelerated privatization of all large Crown corporations,
Supply
including Petro-Canada, Atomic Energy, CN, Marine Atlantic, VIA Rail and CMHC; and to promote technological innovation and research and development marketing, establish a program for privatizing federal government laboratories, especially those working in agriculture, energy and advanced materials.

Radical realignment of budget allocations in the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs away from paternalism and the Ottawa bureaucracy towards selfgovernment and local native initiatives; removal of funding for interest and lobby groups; additional cutbacks in the overseas offices of the Department of External Affairs including the sale of unnecessary houses and apartments for ambassadors, consuls general and senior officials as well as curtailment of travel, perks and expense entitlements of officials; a major restructuring of government controls on departmental spending, including the introduction of departmental internal audits, streamlining of middle management and responsibility accounting based on performance; a review of parliamentary and civil service pensions with a view to eliminating anomalies with the private sector and unfair indexed allowances; cutbacks to the environmental green plan with cost savings partly compensated by market-based incentives, especially for new technologies and support for small business; phase-out of agricultural subsidies and substitution of a new policy of export-based trade promotion; a phased program of civil service cutbacks of 25,000, more than half by attrition during the life of the next Parliament; a parliamentary review of all tax expenditures, that is tax write-offs with a view to tax simplification and fairness.
That is my position on the budget.
The next point, and this is the genuinely mischievous aspect of this motion from the hon. member for Willow-dale, is his implication that my use of the strong language in last Friday's debate was in some way critical of the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Finance's budget.
The Minister of Finance entered elected life almost 25 years ago. It will be his 25th anniversary in Parliament on June 25 of this year, having been elected in 1968 after

serving as a political worker for some time and having had a successful career as a farmer and a businessman.
The Minister of Finance has served, in the words of more than one journalist, as minister of everything in the Government of Canada. In reality he has been the chief operating officer of the government, at least since June 1986. The minister served as transport critic and chairman of the PC committee on transportation and communications prior to being appointed Minister of Transport in the 1979 Clark government and Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board.
In June 1986 he was promoted to Deputy Prime Minister and was also named government House leader and President of the Privy Council. During that year he initiated and developed the highly successful western diversification program.
The member for Vegreville became President of the Treasury Board on August 27, 1987 which brought new responsibilities relating to government expenditures and labour management relations.
On March 31, 1988 he was named Minister Responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs and relinquished his Treasury Board duties.
In September 1988 the member for Vegreville was appointed Minister of Agriculture. In a cabinet reorganization on January 30, 1989 he retained the positions of Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture. In the agricultural portfolio he spearheaded legislation designed to bring economic stability to Canada's agricultural community. The Farm Income Protection Act received Royal Assent on April 11, 1991.
The member for Vegreville was named Minister of Finance on April 21, 1991, retaining the position of Deputy Prime Minister. He serves as vice-chairman of the priorities and planning committee of the cabinet and is a member of the operations committee.
He is vice-chairman of the security and intelligence committee, sits on Treasury Board and is an ex officio member of the cabinet committees on economic and trade policy, environment, foreign and defence policy and human resources.
That is the official c.v. To round out the description of this man whom I have had the honour of knowing for over two decades I will say that he is a man characterized by humility, loyalty, sheer integrity and strength of
character, and unrelenting dedication to whatever task is before him. He is an outstanding political mentor.
We have had some criticism brought forward by hon. members during the course of this debate. The member for Winnipeg South Centre has suggested there has been some sniping on my part toward the Minister of Finance. Nothing could be further from the truth. This is the exasperated last gasp of a frustrated tentative leadership pretender of his own party.
We ought to examine the opposition record, particularly the record of the Official Opposition, with regard to government restraint because these are the people who purport to be experts on the issue of restraint and are criticising the budget that is before us.
I would remind hon. members that the Liberals voted against the Spending Control Act, a law that places a limit on federal government spending. That was Bill C-56. They voted against making the Public Service more efficient and responsive. That was Bill C-26. Other measures in that bill gave women, natives, persons with disabilities and visible minorities better chances to be hired and promoted.
There is more. Listen. The Liberals voted against ending the 1991 Public Service strike, and in so doing they also voted against a freeze on MPs' salaries. That was Bill C-29. They voted against winding down six Crown corporations that duplicated work done elsewhere. That was Bill C-63.
Besides all that, they voted down seven other bills which cut spending to keep the deficit down, Bill C-19, Bill C-26 and Bill C-69 in the second session and Bill C-ll, Bill C-20, Bill C-32 and Bill C-76 in the third session.
Not once has that mob ever voted in favour of spending cuts. Each time they voted against spending cuts.
In the realm of privatization, they voted against privatizing Nordion and Theratronics. They voted against allowing the federal government to sell its shares in Telesat Canada. They voted against the privatization of Petro-Canada.
On social policy, the Liberals voted against the new child tax benefit. This new benefit is better targeted to low and middle income families than the programs it replaced. They voted against improving unemployment insurance maternity benefits and against making job training a major focus of the UI system. They voted

against new rules which will better manage our immigration system.
They voted against setting up the Canadian transportation accident investigation and safety board. They voted against establishing a federal environmental assessment process. They voted against improvements to the equalization program that would provide $600 million over two years to the seven less wealthy provinces that qualify under the program.
Those members voted against a $24 million increase in transfer payments to Yukon. They voted against meeting the costs of Canadian participation in the gulf war. They voted against $164 million in assistance for fishers affected by the northern cod moratorium.
This Official Opposition is bankrupt of policy, bereft of ideas and becalmed in bemusement. What about the other opposition? I think the hon. member for Yukon would be well prepared to preside over a scaled down cabinet. At the rate she is losing her caucus members she would have just about 20 at about the right time.
I want to dwell on a couple of aspects of what this budget provides us with. My position on the budget is clear. I said on April 26 that what this budget gives those of us who are seeking the leadership of the Progressive Conservative Party is a springboard that has lots of bounce to it to move forward and reduce government spending further, as Canadians are now requesting and our economic reality dictates.
The Official Opposition prefers to ignore this reality. Its voting record on the very many significant restraint measures, as I have illustrated, is the proof.
The real disgrace is the voting record of members opposite. Even in the New Democratic Party Governments of Ontario and British Columbia there is a recognition that fiscal restraint is imperative if we are to meet the challenges ahead of us.
We have an opportunity in the coming years to complete the reversal of the overspending habits this government inherited in 1984. This government, this Minister of Finance and his predecessor, the current Minister for International Trade, have succeeded in changing conventional wisdom in this country. Canadians know that reducing government expenditures is

essential to our future. This is a legacy that I am proud to carry forward.

This Whip is prepared to gather the Progressive Conservative Party together to provide for another generation of leadership for this country, to go on to win for Canadians a better future in company with the hon. member for Sherbrooke, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, the members for Halton-Peel and Etobicoke-Lakeshore and a host of others from across this nation.
I wish to advise you, Mr. Speaker, and other members of the House that I will be voting against this silly, foolish, scabrous and mischievous motion.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to a litany of all the measures against which the Official Opposition in its rightful role has voted against.

The Canadian public will be pleased, and I say that with some sarcasm; to note that the member opposite and his colleagues voted for an increase in income taxes, which totalled $26,967 billion in 1984, to $61,222 billion in 1992. In nominal dollars that is an increase of 127 per cent.
That is what the government member opposite voted for. He voted for a 20 per cent increase in the relative revenue for government from income taxes. What he also voted for and what all of his government colleagues voted for was a 33 per cent drop in corporate taxes, in relative terms, from 1992 to 1984.
The other thing that he and all of his government colleagues voted for in the last nine years was a declining rate of GDP growth.
They voted for measures that caused the rate of growth of the GDP in this country to go from 4.8 per cent in real growth in 1985 to 3.5 per cent in 1986, to 4.2 per cent in 1987, to 3 per cent in 1988, to 2.3 per cent in 1989, to negative .5 per cent in 1990, to negative 1.7 per cent in growth in 1991 and to a mere .9 per cent growth in 1992.

miserably. Inflation and unemployment would get worse, interest rates would rise even more, Canada would price itself out of world markets and recovery would be postponed". He let her rip. We in this party do believe that the deficit has to be dealt with. We believe that measures have to be taken to reduce the national debt not by cutting alone or by cutting willy-nilly every measure whether it is one that will produce revenue or one that does not produce revenue.
We need to have a strategy for economic growth which this budget does not have. We must have a strategy for job creation which this budget does not have.
This budget accepts bold face, standing right there in the budget, that the unemployment rate will be near 11 per cent until 1995 and remain high until 1998. The Minister of Finance blatantly stated that in the House but the budget contained no strategy to deal with that horrendous situation and no strategy for economic growth.
How do we produce the revenue we need when we have such large numbers of people unemployed? When balancing a budget whether it is a home budget, an individual budget or the budget of a corporation, we can do it in two ways: by cutting some expenditures by increasing your revenues, by having a strategy for growth and for profits. We just do not cut and do nothing about the growth side, the revenue side. As a matter of fact we do not cut to the extent that we hurt the growth side,
that we kill the growth side. That is what this government is doing.
It is cutting so indiscriminately, it is so negative in its approach to the economy, so small c conservative, still following the policies of Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher and Brian Mulroney of course, that great triumvirate, that it is concentrated to the ignorance of all other pertinent matters which come to play in the economic development of the country and it is concentrating just on these cuts.
As I say those policies that the government has been putting to this House over the last five years are not working. They are not ending up with people in jobs paying taxes or companies producing goods and services.
On the other hand, what is happening as a result of this government's strategy? People are collecting unemployment insurance benefits and welfare. The more it puts people out of work the more people there are collecting unemployment insurance and the more people there are collecting welfare.
I ask the government how this helps dealing with the national deficit and the national debt. Should it not have a strategy whereby those people that are on UI and collecting welfare are put back to work so they can be paying taxes and so that companies instead of going into bankruptcy will be making profits and paying taxes?
This does not mean that taxes have to be raised to deal with the deficit or bring in new taxes. If we had people at work, if we could bring down that unemployment rate and bring back some economic prosperity with the very same tax rates, revenue would increase in a very substantial way and then the deficit problems would be on the way to being solved.
Of course we have to cut out fat and we have to live within our means but we also need a plan to stimulate growth, jobs and investment. When an individual, any one of us, or our families are deep in debt we cut out the frills. We may shift from a high price car to a low price car. A renter may shift from a larger house to one that is more acceptable to their budget.

We do not sell our tools. We do not cut out our transportation which gets us to work. We do not cut out our night courses which will help us upgrade our skills. We do not sell our house altogether and go and live on relief. We do not take our children out of school. We continue to do those things that we need to do to earn an income. We have to continue to buy our tools, to upgrade our trades, to get to work whether it is by car or by subway or by bus or whatever.
My point is this. As a nation we have to continue to invest in those things which will bring in the revenue, bring in the profits, bring in the taxation at the ordinary rates that will put the country back to work.
I have harped over and over again about the municipal infrastructure program. Here we have a program which was agreed to by all the municipalities in Canada, a program to renew municipal infrastructure: roads, bridges, sewers, water purification, sewage treatment and so on.

That plan alone would have not only renewed municipal infrastructure but it would have renewed these cities to attract business investment, to attract commerce and it would also have put thousands and thousands of people back to work.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me the opportunity to speak to my hon. colleague's motion.
My hon. colleague opposite calls for a system of multi-modal transportation terminals and rail links between airports and business centres. It is clear that multi-modal terminals could be given a more important profile in the development of an efficient transportation system. These terminals could involve many modes: intercity and urban bus, rail, commuter rail, subways, taxis and, in some instances, ferries. The terminal would thus become a focal point for both intercity and regional transportation, with a primary function to be to facilitate the transfer of passengers and baggage from one mode to another.
It might be interesting and instructive to set out what multi-modal transportation means in practical terms. Such a facility would be used in one of two ways by the carriers involved: either competitive or complementary. In the competitive form of relationship the carriers compete for the same traveller, whereas in the complementary form one mode brings customers to the other.
We can see that three levels of joint development are possible, requiring successively greater co-operation and co-ordination between the parties involved.
The first level is a simple joint use of facilities where each carrier uses the same facility and pays a pro-rated share of the total terminal costs.
May 4, 1993

The second level of development is the integration of service, which involves arranging schedules so that arrivals and departures allow for transfer from one mode to another.
The last level is that of joint operation in which daily terminal operations are fully integrated.
The underlying philosophy of such integrated transportation facilities and services would be that the modes must complement one another and be able to act as one large unified system. The degree of integration would necessarily have to be high, encompassing not only a joint transportation terminal but also common ticketing and integrated management.
A true multi-modal terminal therefore requires the carriers and terminal operators to work together to produce a more efficient and convenient interface function. This co-operation may include such items as joint scheduling, common management, coordinated fare structures and cost sharing.
The advantages of such arrangements are obvious. In the rail mode, for instance, a multi-modal terminal would raise its profile in the community and enable the industry to operate more economically.
There are some disadvantages though for a carrier. While one would expect that in most cases a carrier may reduce its operating costs, it may find that in other situations it has incurred certain new terminal costs. It may also find that it has lost control over some costs as it is committed to a terminal which it does not entirely control.
In many European countries and some American cities we do find examples where all modes of transport are located under one roof. Additionally, there can be a direct bus and/or rail link between the terminal and the airport.
One may ask why such an integrated transportation infrastructure has developed in Europe. There are many reasons. Some are certainly historical, including a reaction to saving space which meant that new types of transportation were added to existing terminals.
The Europeans and Americans are not alone in then-support of multi-modal terminals. Here in Canada the idea of intermodal integration of transportation facilities and services is already strongly supported by section 3 of the National Transportation Act, 1987 which calls for a
Private Members' Business
network of viable and effective transportation services making the best use of all available modes at the lowest cost.
That is not what we have!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
As I was saying, for my colleague opposite, there is already a basis in section 3 of the 1987 act, and I would ask him to refer to it.
Mr. Speaker, I am not unsupportive of such an objective. It should be recognized though that the establishment of specific facilities and services is a matter that can surely be worked out by carriers and other directly involved parties. In other words, inter-mo-dalism should not be a forced solution. Inter-modalism is considered in federal plans for transportation facilities and services where that can be done. For example, the federal-provincial feasibility study into high-speed rail is specifically looking at the feasibility of linkages with other modes of transport, including access to airports and urban business centres, just as the hon. member wishes.
As well, the National Transportation Act Review Commission has recommended that inter-modalism be specifically recognized in section 3 of the National Transportation Act as forming an integral aspect of transportation policy.
We also see that the Royal Commission on National Passenger Transportation recommended that all agreements for the sale or lease of federal transportation infrastructure should include provisions that oblige the operating authority to grant open access to all intermodal connectors on equal terms and conditions.
These recommendations are under review by the government. On this point, the Minister of Transport has established a working group to review these two important reports, and has asked for a status report to be available this fall.
For its part, VIA, as our national rail carrier, is poised to pursue the establishment of multimodal terminals wherever appropriate opportunities exist. It must be remembered that VIA cannot do so without the co-operation of not only other carriers but operating authorities as well. For example, CN, not VIA, is the owner of Montreal's Central Station. In Toronto, CN and CP own the main station. These are two of the largest terminals served by VIA.

May 4, 1993
Private Members' Business
It may come as a surprise to some but there are already cases where VIA has successfully negotiated the establishment of a multi-modal transportation facility. For example, its Pacific Central Station in Vancouver will be officially opened next month. VTA Rail and Greyhound Lines of Canada, as well as other bus and train services, will operate out of this one central location. In this particular case, VIA management recognized that participation made good business sense and they took advantage of the opportunity that was presented.
We believe that this arrangement will benefit rail and bus passengers by providing modem amenities. By sharing the facilities, Greyhound and its partners and VIA Rail will all realize cost efficiencies.
I am also pleased to say that the newly structured VIA is deliberately focused to rethink the conduct of business for passenger rail, not only within funding levels set by the federal government but, more importantly, to meet the challenges of increasing its passenger volume while pursuing a cost effective practice.
Much of this success is due to VIA's own awareness of its product, image and service to the travelling public. In other words, I believe that market conditions must be the basis of rational business decisions about the practicalities and feasibility of multi-modalism, and it is about time that we move in that direction.
In conclusion, the development of a system of multimodal terminals will depend on the objectives of all parties concerned: VIA, bus carriers, air carriers, transit authorities, other operating authorities and definitely not forgetting the final decision-maker, the public. Whatever we might say, although the idea is interesting, it is up to all those concerned, to these partners, to move in that direction. Ultimately the market and the public will decide.

southern Ontario in terms of the provision of aviation services.

On the other hand we saw this national capital eliminate its tracks downtown and eliminating the station. It was moved out to a decent cab-ride distance, whereas it was much more accessible to people here. It was really multi-modal in the sense that urban transit was connected to it for members of Parliament. They could just walk up to the Hill to their office and so forth.
All these kinds of things make sense. It is an efficient use of energy, there is less damage to the environment and it is easier for the people who are using the services. ticketing. It specifies the language of service and a lot of other things. The Canadian National Railways Act has all sorts of parameters in there as well but nothing for VIA. It is an orphan, as my colleague has described it.
Part of the problem that we have had over the last number of years is that without legislative authority VIA Rail is subject to the whims of the Minister of Transport or in a lot of cases to the Minister of Finance who has cut and slashed rail passenger services in this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the pursuit of an enhanced passenger rail service and the establishment of multi-modal passenger transportation terminals proposed by my hon. friend from Regina-Lumsden, these are not new concepts and it is not the first time that he has proposed these things.
With regard to the former we are now exploring the possibilities of high-speed rail whereas our experience with the latter in Canada, namely the multi-modal terminals, has been somewhat varied.
At the outset I would like to indicate that the federal government certainly has no problems with encouraging private business interests in the development of such
systems. In fact, I am sure the hon. member is no doubt aware that provisions of the National Transportation Act encourage the development of a network of viable and effective transportation services for making the best use of all available modes at the lowest total cost.
It should also be noted that while the government supports the principle outlined in the legislation, this government is of the view that it is up to private carriers, passengers and business interests, and not up to the government, to build and support such passenger system terminals.
In other words, without the involvement of the private sector such pursuits are not possible as passenger transportation costs are essentially time based. There has to be clear evidence of time cost advantages for passengers and profits to be made by carriers prior to the infusion of the massive capital required to build both high-speed trains and multi-modal passenger terminals.
They build airports.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
The hon. member says: "They build airports". In fact the Vancouver airport has been turned over to a private group and the expansion of the third runway at the Vancouver International Airport will be paid for mainly out of an airport departure fee. They started to collect the airport departure fee as of last Saturday, May 1.
It can be argued that in Canada we already have evidence of a multi-modal approach to passenger transportation. For example intercity buses and cabs service airports, train stations and bus terminals. There is even co-operation between the bus industry and VIA. This is particularly the case in the maritime provinces where efforts have been made since 1990 in the restructuring of VIA to enhance other connections between remaining passenger services.
As well there is the example of the Ontario Northland Commission which operates both rail passenger and bus services in northern Ontario. There is also the distinctive double-decker GO transport system which runs in conjunction with an extensive bus feeder network. I might add it carries many thousands of people every day in and out of Toronto.



May 4, 1993

It should be remembered that not all multi-modal efforts necessarily are limited to rail or bus transportation. For example, the Acadian lines in Nova Scotia operate several of its intercity bus services through the Halifax International Airport.
The hon. member is no doubt aware that the corridor between Quebec City and Windsor has been the subject of numerous studies with a view to ascertaining the feasibility of implementing high-speed rail in the Quebec to Windsor corridor. To date we have no conclusive results.
The Ontario-Quebec rapid train task force report released in June 1991 represents the most comprehensive work on the subject. In its report the task force concluded that on the basis of its study it was not possible to make a final decision with respect to the project and recommended further study.
The Governments of Canada, Ontario and Quebec have established a federal-provincial team with specific tasks. The team has undertaken a pre-feasibility study using the Ontario-Quebec report as a starting point. This exercise currently under way consists of various component studies that are examining such detailed issues as routing, technology, forecasting, institutional options, industrial strategy, modal impacts and studies. A report is expected in the fall. I am sure it will prove of much interest and value in this ongoing debate.
With specific reference to the member's suggestion that the government should build rail links between airports and urban business centres, I would like to point to one of the studies done in that regard in 1990. The National Research Council carried out a preliminary analysis of an integrated multi-modal chiefly air-rail passenger transportation approach in the high density Toronto-Ottawa-Montreal corridor. The air link is a recognized progression in the evolution of commercial passenger transportation. Indeed it is currently operational in Germany. The Deutsche Bundestag and the German Federal Railway have closely integrated its high speed rail services with those of Lufthansa, the German national airline. This in effect incorporates the benefits of multi-modal with high-speed rail.
In its preliminary analysis the NRC study looked at high-speed rail interconnections between Pearson, Uplands, Mirabel and Dorval airports. Under this concept the rail link would be used to shuttle passengers
Private Members' Business
between airports for improved access to national, international and long distance flights.
Downtown access to Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal would be provided by extensions of existing urban transit networks such as subways and/or bus trimodal modes. These can be at or near airports with the rail terminals being provided with extensive parking facilities for automobiles.
There is one serious disadvantage to this kind of motion. Even if we can ignore all the jurisdictional questions like provincial responsibilities for commuter transportation, and assuming we can convince all the municipalities that such a route invariably traverses, there is still one small problem and that problem is money and more specifically taxpayers' money.
I know the hon. member opposite and his party often suggest that money is not the problem. They suggest it is just a case of having the will to do it and the money will find itself. In reality governments do not have a lot of money and essentially must be very frugal as to how they spend the money. We in government have to make tough decisions about fiscal responsibility and we will continue to do so.
In closing I must say that the pursuit of multi-modal terminals and high-speed rail links are complex matters that require further assessment before any decisions regarding enhancement of passenger rail services can be made. Those decisions will not be possible without informed and co-operative input from the other levels of government and the private sector.
Suggesting the federal government should take on these responsibilities and pay I do not think is in the cards at this time. Therefore I cannot support the motion. I thank the House very much for the opportunity to speak to the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to address the motion of the member for Regina-Lumsden concerning the enhancement of passenger service. I want to congratulate the member for all his years of service and wish him luck and Godspeed. I am wondering if this debate might merit mention in the biography I understand he is writing right now. Certainly we will hear a lot about transportation issues in that biography.

May 4, 1993
Private Members' Business
As we have heard, the objectives are in themselves very worthy of pursuit, and I will certainly not argue to the contrary. I do, however, have a concern about any proposal regarding the federal government's financial participation in their achievement.
As we have witnessed in the budget of April 26, funding available for VIA Rail, our national rail passenger carrier, has had its reference levels reduced in order to help address this country's serious deficit problem. It was not an easy decision. Nevertheless we must not be turned aside from our program of deficit reduction which is designed to ensure economic security for all Canadians in the future. This government is not afraid to take such difficult decisions, and they are very difficult decisions.
What this must mean is that the federal financial resources available for rail passenger services must necessarily, at least in the foreseeable future, be limited to projects which are commercially viable.
To illustrate my point, let us examine the funding reduction that will be applied to the operations of VIA Rail Canada. Starting in 1995-96 the federal subsidy to the Crown corporation will be reduced to produce total savings of $250 million by the end of 1997-98. There is no doubt that the government is providing VIA Rail management with a major challenge. How this challenge will be met will be a subject of future corporate plans. What we must realize now is that there is every reason to believe the corporation will meet this challenge with success as it has met past challenges with success. We know this by experience.
Allow me to put our present position into context by returning to the challenge this government placed before VIA management in 1989 when it was announced that we would reduce federal subsidies. The actual amounts represented went from a high of $607 million in 1988-89 to $343 million, the current level, in 1993-94. A subsidy of $607 million was reduced to $343 million, still a huge subsidy.
To meet this challenge the federal government gave VIA a new mandate in 1989. That mandate was to prepare and implement a new business plan which respected the corporation's new funding levels and
ultimately would see VIA operate services in a way that imposes an even lower burden on Canadian taxpayers.
VIA has met this objective. With every successive year since the network restructuring of January 15, 1990 the corporation has succeeded in continuing to improve product quality. At the same time it has lowered the cost of the rail passenger network to Canadian taxpayers. This success has been achieved despite a downturn in the travel market in recent years.
Mr. Lawrence Hanigan, VIA's former chairman, was reported by the press as saying that in hindsight the decision'to reduce the size of the company and cut some unprofitable lines in January 1990 was painful but right.
He said:
We have been able to improve productivity, use better equipment
and improve the quality of services on board -All of this is paying off
right now. That's why, with less money, we're able to do more.
VIA's 1992 annual report, which was tabled in the House on April 27, 1993 shows that revenues which totalled $155.8 million in 1992 represent an increase of $5.7 million, that is a 3.8 per cent increase over the prior year. This occurred during a recession.
In terms of government subsidy, operating funding per passenger mile decreased in 1992 to 41.2 cents from 43 cents in 1991 and 52 cents the year before that. How did the corporation achieve this? It did so through improved customer service, various productivity improvements and the fostering of a team-building spirit within the company, and that is important.
To further expand on this matter let me quote from Mr. Lawless' address of February 16, 1993 to the Standing Committee on Transport and it reads as follows-I am sorry I am missing that quote.
As it has done in the past, VIA Rail will review options for expenditure reductions and develop a business plan which will respond to reduced financial support while taking into account all such measures that are available to it to improve its bottom line. This will require some difficult adjustments. Nevertheless, the corporation has publicly stated that affected employees will be treated fairly.

Furthermore, while it is premature to consider service adjustments at this point Mr. Lawless has been quoted in the press as stating that VIA is committed to preserving the national network.
I want to state that while we have not underestimated the challenge now presented to VIA, we have not underestimated VIA's capacity to meet that challenge.
To sum up my reaction to the hon. member's motion, in light of my comments about VIA I have to say that while enhancing rail services and increasing multi-mo-dalism is a laudable goal we must always keep before us our first priority, which is to the taxpayers of this country.
That is not to say that present systems cannot be enhanced. Indeed they can. However we must be wary of any proposal that amounts to a carte blanche to spend money.
The opposition day after day wants to spend more money on services to buy people's votes. As Premier Wells found out last night, as the people of Newfoundland stated last night, the taxpayers do not want to be bought with their own money. They want us to keep on facing the challenges that we have before us, to improve service, to improve productivity and to improve quality.
We have done that with VIA Rail. Those decisions were difficult. I applaud the hon. member for his motion but at the present time I cannot offer it the support I would like to because of our financial constraints.
