Mr. Speaker, this is a private member's motion put by the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden which suggests that the government should consider the advisability of enhancing passenger rail service, establish a system of multi-modal passenger transportation terminals, build rail links between airports and urban business centres and between certain airports such as Pearson International in Toronto and Hamilton airport.
My perspective I guess is from someone who represents a sparsely populated area on the southern prairies, an area which in fact lost its passenger rail service a few
Private Members' Business
years ago, a passenger rail service that was rather sporadic at best. We had one train in and one train out each day. Sometimes it arrived on time and sometimes it did not. I believe that on average three or four people boarded and three or four people got off at the various stops within my constituency.
I believe I received two representations from my entire constituency lamenting the loss of that passenger service. The reason was because even then, a few years ago, people and certainly my constituents were sensitized to the need to deal with government spending and government deficit. They were cognizant of the kind of deficits that passenger rail service in Canada were running. I have forgotten the numbers now but I believe that every time someone steps on a train in this country it costs the taxpayer something in excess of $100.1 maybe understating the figure when I say that. So I have considerable difficulty coming from that background to find an enormous amount of enthusiasm for this motion.
This motion sort of flies in the face of contemporary thinking in this country. It speaks about enhancing passenger rail service, establishing a system of transportation terminals and building rail links. Those may be very fine hopes and aspirations but at the end of the day someone has to pay for them. I have a feeling the source the hon. member who put this motion has in mind is the Government of Canada and ultimately the taxpayers. I really would question the affordability.
It is unfortunate that the cost of passenger rail travel and freight movement has become so expensive. I would like to quote from volume I of the National Transportation Act Review Commission which deals with one important aspect of the cost of rail service. It is interesting because it talks about labour productivity. While it indicates that railway labour productivity has improved in Canada it has not done so to the same extent as in the United States.
For example, just comparing railways: In 1991 the productivity for an employee at CP Rail was only 60 per cent of the level achieved by the employees at seven leading U.S. railroads. CN employees stood at 56 per cent of their U.S. counterparts. I do not have the figures relating to VIA and Amtrak and passenger rail service in the United States, but I would be surprised if there were substantial differences.

May 4, 1993
Private Members' Business
One of the really major expenditures has been the cost of labour downsizing associated with severance payments. For example, the NTA report indicates that in 1991 the cost to CN of employee separations amounted to $94 million. CP Rail wrote off $251 million in restructuring charges that same year. The report indicates that severance payments of this generosity obviously erode the economies achieved by downsizing. This situation should not have been allowed to develop.
It goes on to point out the differential between wages in the trucking sector and wages in the railway sector. The average railway employee receives something in the order of $43,000 per year in Canada.
The commission asked why railway labour compensation is so high. They say it may have been due in part to the regulatory protection given to the railways over many decades, in part the inability and/or unwillingness of railway management to countenance strikes and in part to the speedy intervention of government on the rare occasions when strikes have occurred. Government railway management and shippers, all unwilling to face
strikes, have played a part in this development, they go on to conclude.
I raise this because it is one of the fundamental problems the rail industry faces in this country, these incredibly high labour costs. Then of course when the companies run the huge loses they come crying to government for more and more in the way of taxpayer involvement.
